findings.description: The bucket declares no server_side_encryption_configuration block, so objects (including the seeded vendor roster) are stored without a customer-controlled or KMS-managed encryption key configuration. This is inconsistent with the audit_trail bucket in the same file, which does use aws:kms.

No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block resource is associated with this bucket and no ACL is declared, so nothing prevents a later bucket policy or object ACL from making the contents (a vendor roster spreadsheet) publicly readable. Every other bucket in the file at least declares an explicit private ACL.
No bucket policy denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false, so objects may be read or written over plain HTTP. None of the buckets in this file enforce TLS.

The ledger export bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration block. Financial ledger data is stored unencrypted at the bucket-default level, with no KMS key and therefore no key-level access control or audit trail on decryption.

No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is attached, so account-level or future object ACLs and policies could expose ledger exports publicly. The private ACL alone does not block subsequent public policy attachment.
Versioning and access logging are configured, but no server_side_encryption_configuration is declared, so model artifacts are stored without an enforced bucket-default encryption policy.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block resource guards this bucket, leaving it open to accidental public exposure through a later policy or object ACL change.

Operational runbooks frequently contain internal hostnames, escalation procedures, and occasionally credentials or recovery steps. The bucket declares no server_side_encryption_configuration, so this content is stored without enforced default encryption.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is associated with the runbooks bucket, so nothing structurally prevents public exposure of internal operational documentation.

The bucket receiving access logs for model_artifacts sets force_destroy = true and has neither MFA delete nor object lock, so a single terraform destroy (or an actor with the pipeline's credentials) can delete all audit evidence. This undermines the integrity of the audit trail an attacker would want to erase.
The audit log bucket has no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block resource. Log-delivery-write buckets containing access records should be explicitly blocked from all public access.

The object is uploaded with no server_side_encryption argument into reports_archive, a bucket with no default encryption, so vendor-roster.xlsx is stored unencrypted. The source file is also committed alongside the Terraform code, placing third-party vendor data in the source repository.
